text:
The wild hemp, also known as marijuana, is an annual plant that grows each year from seed. The leaves are compound with each leaf having an odd number of separate leaflets—usually five to eleven but commonly seven.

Each leaflet has notched or "saw-toothed" edges.
When they flower, some marijuana plants can be recognized as male and others as female. The male plant has many small greenish-yellow flowers that produce pollen. After shedding pollen, the male plant turns yellow, withers, and dies. The flowers of the female plant are less conspicuous. But after pollination the female plant becomes bushy and heavy with seeds, and many remain green and vigorous until frost. At maturity marijuana plants may vary in size from three to ten feet tall and may sometimes be even taller.
The stem is rough, somewhat grooved, and generally branched. Plants growing in the open have more lower branches and are more bushy than plants growing in crowded areas. The entire plant may feel rough. Leaves, stems, and seeds give a distinctive odor when crushed.
The marijuana plant has a main tap root up to about 8 inches long.

The main root has many smaller roots along it.
Marijuana seeds may begin germinating and plants appear about the last part of April or early May. All the seeds in the soil do not germinate at one time, and some plants may begin growing at various times during the season when soil moisture and temperatures are favorable for seed germination.
